# Diagnosing Serpentine Belt Melting and Black Residue

Encountering a serpentine belt that has melted, leaving the engine bay coated in black gunk, is a critical failure mode that demands immediate attention. In your case, the 2013 Buick Verano's inability to charge the battery points directly to an alternator driven by this belt system. The visual evidence of a melted belt and pervasive black residue indicates a thermal event severe enough to compromise the integrity of rubber components. This is rarely a simple maintenance issue; it is a symptom of catastrophic friction or electrical failure.

The primary suspect in scenarios involving melted belts and dark, tar-like deposits is a seized accessory bearing. When an idler pulley, tensioner, or the alternator bearing seizes, the friction between the rubber belt and the metal sheave generates immense heat. This heat exceeds the thermal threshold of the EPDM (ethylene propylene diene monomer) rubber used in automotive belts. As the rubber degrades, it carbonizes, creating the black sludge you are observing. The belt does not simply break; it chars and softens, often fusing to the pulley grooves before snapping or slipping off entirely.

If the alternator bearing failed first, the shaft could have locked up while the rest of the engine continued to rotate at high RPMs. This creates a grinding scenario where the belt is forced against a stationary component. The resulting heat flash can melt the belt's internal cords and cover it in carbonized debris. It is crucial to inspect all pulleys for play or roughness before removing the belt, even if one pulley appears visually intact. A seized bearing on an otherwise pristine-looking pulley will destroy a new belt within minutes of startup.

The black gunk itself is likely a mixture of carbonized rubber and oxidized grease from the failed bearing seals. When a bearing fails, its internal lubricant escapes, mixing with the hot rubber dust created by the abrasion. This slurry can coat nearby components like the alternator housing, water pump, or radiator shroud. While this residue might seem merely cosmetic, it acts as an insulator and can attract moisture, leading to corrosion on electrical connectors or short circuits in sensitive areas. Cleaning this area requires more than just a quick wipe; you need to remove the carbon build-up to ensure proper airflow and prevent future tracking issues.

Replacement involves removing the tensioner pulley to relieve pressure on the belt. This allows access to the old, melted remains. Do not attempt to salvage any portion of the original belt or reuse the tensioner if it has been subjected to such extreme heat. The structural integrity of the tensioner's spring and pivot point may be compromised even if they appear functional at first glance.

Once the new belt is installed, you must verify that all pulleys spin freely with no lateral play. This step is non-negotiable. If a bearing was the root cause, replacing only the belt will result in immediate failure upon the next drive cycle. You may need to swap out the alternator or tensioner assembly depending on your specific model year configuration. Ensure the new belt is routed correctly; incorrect routing can lead to premature wear and potential belt throw-off events under load.

If you are performing this repair yourself, take the opportunity to inspect the wiring harness near the alternator. The heat generated by the bearing failure may have damaged insulation on nearby wires. Checking for melted insulation or exposed conductors is a vital safety step that often gets overlooked when focused solely on the belt and bearings.
